hero.alt: Three-dimensional surface plot of two multimode solitons of unequal amplitude propagating along a graded-index fibre, colliding, and continuing unchanged — intensity mapped to height and to colour on a black ground.
hero.caption: Two multimode solitons colliding in a graded-index fibre.

figures.title: Where a soliton's noise comes from, and where it goes
figures.alt: Five-panel schematic: a Kerr resonator and its comb; field-level fluctuations; projection onto the four collective coordinates amplitude, frequency, timing and phase; a diagram of the couplings between them; and the resulting RIN, timing phase noise and common-mode phase noise spectra.
figures.caption: Field fluctuations are projected onto the four coordinates a soliton actually has — amplitude, frequency, timing, phase — and the couplings between them (amplitude–phase, Raman-assisted transfer, frequency-to-timing conversion) decide the noise you can measure at the output.

figures.title: Soliton crystals and the fluctuations a single pulse carries
figures.alt: Left: a parametrically driven Kerr ring with several solitons, and the comb harmonics produced by crystal orderings labelled PPNN, PPPN, PNPN. Right: amplitude, phase and timing fluctuations of one soliton, and the corresponding frequency-shift fluctuation of the comb.
figures.caption: n solitons circulating at equal spacing print n free spectral ranges onto the comb, and the phase pattern of the crystal decides which harmonics survive. On the right, the four fluctuations a single pulse carries.

figures.title: A temporal cavity plus a spatial cavity
figures.alt: Three panels: a fibre ring with a phase modulator producing a temporal cavity soliton; a Fabry-Perot cavity with Kerr media producing a spatial soliton; and the two combined into a graded-index spatiotemporal cavity supporting multimode solitons.
figures.caption: Confine light in time with dispersion, confine it in space with a graded-index fibre, and do both at once: the result is a multimode cavity soliton, a pulse localized in all three dimensions.

figures.title: What makes a multimode soliton
figures.alt: Three panels: a temporal soliton in single-mode fibre balancing chromatic dispersion against nonlinearity; a spatial soliton balancing diffraction against nonlinearity; and a spatiotemporal multimode soliton in a graded-index fibre where chromatic and modal dispersion balance nonlinearity together.
figures.caption: A temporal soliton balances dispersion against nonlinearity; a spatial one balances diffraction against it. In a graded-index fibre both happen at once, and modal dispersion joins in.

figures.title: Why a nanolaser mode-locks at all
figures.alt: Left: a free particle in a box compared with a harmonic oscillator, and a Fabry-Perot cavity compared with a chirped distributed Bragg reflector. Right: the equally spaced Hermite-Gaussian modes of the photonic potential, and the resulting pulse circulating in the cavity.
figures.caption: A photonic-crystal nanolaser is a harmonic oscillator, not a box. Its Hermite–Gaussian modes are equally spaced in frequency, so they lock — and the pulse period is set by the potential, not by the cavity length.
